description: Cosmic Explorers Pakistan is a student team participating in the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge. We are interested in space science, astronomy, astrophysics, and using NASA data to explore real-world problems. We welcome teammates who enjoy research, data analysis, coding, design, and presenting ideas. Beginners are welcome if they are motivated to learn, collaborate, and contribute. We are looking for creative and dedicated team members for the Universal Event.
summary:
Cosmic Explorer is an interactive archive of 18 robotic Mars missions, from Mariner 4 in 1964 to the rovers and spacecraft exploring Mars today. Visitors can search, filter and explore each mission's history, spacecraft details, instruments, discoveries, images, videos and official NASA and ESA sources.

The website is built with React, TypeScript and Supabase. Its information is based on cited sources, with missing, estimated or conflicting figures clearly identified. The AI assistant answers questions using the archive's records and directs users to the relevant sources for verification.

The project also includes our research paper, Beyond the Mission: The Fate of Discarded Mars Landing Equipment, which examines what happens to Perseverance's heat shield and descent stage after landing and why these components matter for future Mars missions.

Cosmic Explorer gives students a way to learn about Mars exploration, examine mission records and understand how scientific information is collected, checked and presented.
details:
Cosmic Explorer: An Interactive Archive of Mars Exploration

1. Project Overview: What It Does and How It Works

Cosmic Explorer is an interactive digital archive documenting 18 robotic Mars missions, from Mariner 4 in 1964 to spacecraft operating in the modern era. It brings decades of Mars exploration history into one centralized platform, making scientific information easier to discover, understand, and explore.

Each mission has a dedicated page containing its launch and arrival dates, spacecraft specifications, instruments, scientific objectives, discoveries, mission status, and other historical information. Visitors can also explore spacecraft photographs, technical structural diagrams, archival documentary footage, and links to official NASA or ESA sources, where available.

The platform features an interactive Mission Explorer that allows visitors to search, filter, and sort missions by mission phase, spacecraft type, operating agency, and status. A keyboard-accessible quick search (Ctrl+K) provides direct access to individual mission records.

Additional features include an Ingenuity flight section featuring an interactive technical drawing, a research and publications section, and an AI-powered chat assistant. The assistant uses curated mission information from the project's database to answer questions about Mars exploration and is instructed to decline questions outside its available records. Visitors are also encouraged to verify its responses using the linked sources.

The platform incorporates our original research study, Beyond the Mission: The Fate of Discarded Mars Landing Equipment. Using Perseverance's heat shield and descent stage as its case study, the research explores the engineering and scientific significance of hardware left behind after a Mars landing. Visitors can access the study through an integrated PDF viewer or a structured web article.

2. Benefits of the Project

  • Centralized scientific information: Brings together information from NASA, JPL, NSSDCA, the Planetary Data System, and ESA, reducing the need to navigate multiple technical databases.
  • Educational accessibility: Makes complex aerospace information easier to explore for students, educators, researchers, and space enthusiasts.
  • Traceable information: Mission records include source references, confidence levels, and curatorial notes, allowing visitors to investigate where information originates and how reliable it is considered.
  • Transparency about uncertainty: Unknown, estimated, and conflicting historical values are identified rather than replaced with unsupported assumptions.
  • Interactive learning: Search tools, filters, spacecraft diagrams, archival footage, and the AI assistant provide different ways to engage with Mars exploration history.
  • Research integration: Connects historical mission documentation with original research, helping visitors explore scientific and engineering questions beyond individual missions.

3. Intended Impact

Our goal is to make Mars exploration history more accessible while encouraging scientific curiosity, research, and critical thinking.

A considerable amount of information about Mars missions is distributed across technical reports, scientific databases, and individual space agency websites. Cosmic Explorer brings this information into a structured environment where visitors can explore missions, understand their contributions, and follow links to the original sources.

We also want to encourage scientific information literacy. By presenting source references, confidence levels, and discrepancies alongside mission data, the platform encourages visitors to question where a fact comes from, how reliable it is, and whether different sources agree.

Our accompanying research extends this purpose by examining an often-overlooked part of planetary exploration: what happens to landing equipment after a spacecraft reaches the Martian surface. Studying this hardware can contribute to understanding landing-system performance, future spacecraft engineering, and the preservation of the Martian environment.

Ultimately, we want Cosmic Explorer to become an educational resource that students can use not only to learn the history of Mars exploration but also to investigate and verify the information behind it.

4. Tools and Technologies Used

Cosmic Explorer was developed using modern web technologies, database infrastructure, and AI integration.

Frontend and Development

    • TypeScript
    • React 19
    • Vite
    • HTML5
    • CSS Modules

Database and Cloud Storage

    • Supabase
    • PostgreSQL
    • Supabase Storage for spacecraft images, technical diagrams, and media assets

Artificial Intelligence

    • Groq API
    • Open-weight gpt-oss-120b model
    • Database-grounded conversational question answering

Additional Technologies

    • PDF.js for integrated research paper viewing
    • HTML5 Canvas for the animated starfield background
    • Google Fonts for typography
    • CSS animations and interactive visual effects

Deployment and Infrastructure

    • Vercel for hosting and deployment
    • Supabase for database and cloud media infrastructure
    • Git and GitHub for version control and project collaboration

Scientific Research Sources

    • NASA Science
    • NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL)
    • NASA Planetary Data System
    • NASA Space Science Data Coordinated Archive (NSSDCA)
    • NASA Technical Reports Server
    • European Space Agency (ESA)

5. Creativity and Innovation

The central idea behind Cosmic Explorer is to combine historical mission documentation, scientific research, interactive exploration, and source transparency into a single experience.

  • Aerospace-inspired experience: Instead of using a conventional educational website layout, we designed the interface around a vintage aerospace dossier aesthetic, featuring a dark cinematic theme and a parchment-inspired light theme.
  • Technical spacecraft illustrations: Structural drawings accompany mission imagery, allowing visitors to explore the engineering and physical design of spacecraft rather than seeing them only as historical photographs.
  • Conversational exploration: The integrated AI assistant allows visitors to investigate mission information through natural-language questions, making the archive easier to navigate.
  • Research within the archive: Our original research paper is integrated directly into the platform, connecting mission records with broader questions about spacecraft engineering and planetary exploration.
  • Interactive mission discovery: Dynamic filtering, sorting, keyboard shortcuts, animated elements, and the Ingenuity technical drawing create an experience that encourages active exploration.
  • Visible scientific uncertainty: One of the project's defining features is its approach to information. Sources, confidence levels, missing values, and conflicting records are presented as part of the archive rather than hidden from visitors.

6. Factors Considered During Development

Our team considered scientific, technical, educational, and practical factors throughout the development process.

Scientific Accuracy and Source Reliability: We prioritized information from authoritative NASA and ESA sources. When historical records contained conflicting figures or incomplete information, we avoided unsupported assumptions. We also disclose that the records have not yet been independently fact-checked, allowing visitors to understand the current verification status.

Accessibility and Usability: We designed the platform for different audiences, including students, researchers, educators, and general visitors. Considerations included keyboard navigation, semantic HTML, reduced-motion preferences, and persistent light and dark theme preferences.

AI Reliability: We recognized that language models can generate inaccurate information. The assistant is therefore designed around curated mission records and instructed to decline questions outside its available information. Source links provide an additional way for visitors to verify answers.

Performance: We aimed to keep the application responsive by avoiding unnecessary dependencies and considering the performance of animations, media, and interactive components.

Security: We used a read-only public database key for browser-side access and took precautions to prevent secret credentials from being exposed in the frontend build.

Scalability: Mission information is stored in structured database records, making it easier to expand the archive with additional missions, images, diagrams, and research materials without redesigning the entire platform.

7. Future Possibilities

Cosmic Explorer is designed with room for further development. Potential improvements include:

  • An interactive 3D Mars globe displaying spacecraft orbits, landing locations, and exploration routes.
  • Live scientific data from active Mars rovers and orbiters.
  • Expanded documentation covering additional historical and future Mars missions.
  • More detailed interactive spacecraft and instrument visualizations.
  • Additional scientific research publications and educational resources.

Our Vision

Cosmic Explorer aims to transform scattered Mars exploration records into an accessible, interactive scientific archive. By bringing mission history, spacecraft engineering, original research, and traceable sources together, we want to help students and visitors understand not only what humanity has discovered about Mars, but also how that knowledge was obtained and verified.

Our ultimate goal is to make learning about planetary exploration more engaging, transparent, and accessible while inspiring curiosity about the future of space exploration.
